you call yourself is a deal between your callback and the source, and Angular isn't part of it. If the source lives longer than the component, the callback keeps running and keeps the destroyed component in memory. End those subscriptions with

A support agent opens a ticket, goes back to the list, and opens another one. By the fifth ticket, every incoming message pops up five identical toasts, and the tab's memory keeps climbing through the shift. The ticket page subscribes to a notification stream in its constructor to show those toasts. Each visit created a page and a subscription; each exit destroyed the page, and none of the subscriptions.

The belief: when Angular destroys a component, it tears down everything that component started, including every subscription it opened. Unsubscribing by hand is a leftover from older Angular versions.
There's real evidence for it. The
pipe unsubscribes when its component is destroyed.
does the same, and so do effects. Most

subscriptions end by themselves because the Observable completes after the response, so code that subscribes to HTTP calls and never unsubscribes rarely shows a problem. After a few years of that, it's easy to conclude that cleanup is the framework's job. It is, but only for the subscriptions the framework made.

A subscription is a reference from the source to your callback, and your callback refers to the component through

HTTP subscriptions end, but not always in time

Observables usually complete once the response arrives, which is why the Angular HTTP guide says there's usually no risk of a memory leak if you don't clean them up. The same guide still strongly recommends cleaning them up when the component is destroyed, for a different reason: a slow response can arrive after the user has left, and the callback then runs against a destroyed component, writing state nobody displays or navigating from a page that's gone. Unsubscribing also aborts a request that's still in flight.

blocks.title: Confirm a leak with a heap snapshot

content.text: In a development build, open the page and leave it a few times, then take a heap snapshot in Chrome's Memory panel, which starts with a garbage collection. Type the component's class name in the Class filter: one instance for a page that's open, or none for a page you left, is healthy. Five means five pages are still reachable, and the Retainers section shows what holds them.
